bp: A modern machine learning system is rarely a single program that reads raw data and instantly becomes a model. A sample may be cleaned, reshaped, filtered, augmented, grouped with other samples, sent through training, and revisited many times as the model changes. The practical question is simple: when someone asks, "Was this particular sample used, when did it move through the system, and are the records still trustworthy?" the system should be able to answer with evidence. This matters for audits, user trust, compliance, debugging, and disputes over data use. Existing transparency often describes the model as a whole: what it predicts, why a prediction may happen, or what kind of architecture it has. This paper aims lower and more concretely, at the life of each individual sample. FG-Trac treats data usage as a chain of recorded events that must be captured, checked, and protected from later rewriting.
wh: The hard part is that pipeline transparency has to follow a moving object. A sample is not just present or absent. It can be transformed during preprocessing, enter training at particular times, influence model states unequally, and leave behind records that someone might later question. A model-level explanation cannot answer those operational questions because it describes the trained system after the fact, not the journey each sample took. A training log can help, but ordinary logs are often incomplete, detached from model checkpoints, or easy to alter without leaving obvious signs. The system also cannot demand that every model architecture or training objective be rewritten, because real organizations use many kinds of models and pipelines. The central tension is between fine-grained evidence and practical adoption: the trace must be detailed enough to audit one sample, but light enough to run across preprocessing and training without damaging predictive performance or imposing excessive computational overhead.
naive: A smart beginner might keep a spreadsheet or database table listing each sample identifier, each preprocessing step, and whether the sample entered training. That would be better than memory, but it would fail as audit evidence. The table might say a sample was used, yet not tie that statement to the model states created during training. It might record broad batches while losing the exact sample-level events that matter in a dispute. It might also be changed later by accident or by a party with an incentive to hide misuse. Another simple approach is to explain the final model, but that answers a different question: why the model behaves as it does, not whether a particular record moved through the pipeline intact.
ap: The paper's central move is to make traceability an explicit layer around the pipeline rather than a custom change inside the model. FG-Trac records sample lifecycle events as samples pass through preprocessing and training. It then links those records to training checkpoints, the saved states of the model at particular moments, so contribution scores are not free-floating claims but are grounded in the actual training process. Finally, it anchors the resulting traces in tamper-evident cryptographic commitments. In plain terms, it writes down the important events, ties them to the moments where the model changed, and seals the record so later alteration becomes detectable. Because the method is model-agnostic, it is meant to work with different architectures and objectives, including the convolutional neural network and multimodal graph learning pipeline used in the experiments.
mech: The mechanism starts with the machine learning pipeline itself: raw samples enter preprocessing, are transformed into a usable form, and then participate in training. FG-Trac adds a recording path alongside that work. For each individual sample, it captures lifecycle events, meaning the concrete moments that say what happened to the sample as it was processed and trained on. During training, the method pays attention to checkpoints, which are saved snapshots of the model's state. Those checkpoints matter because they let the trace connect a sample's presence to particular stages of learning rather than only to a final model. FG-Trac computes contribution scores that are explicitly grounded in those checkpoints, so the output can say more than "this sample was in the dataset"; it can provide an account of how the sample was used as the model evolved. The recorded events and derived scores are then turned into cryptographic commitments, which function like tamper-evident seals: someone can later verify that the trace being shown is the same trace that was anchored earlier. The final product is a complete, auditable data-usage history for a sample, including whether it was used, when it was processed, and whether the corresponding records remain intact over time.
math: Several mathematical ideas are doing work here. The first is event modeling: the messy motion of a sample through a pipeline is turned into a sequence of discrete records, each saying that a particular thing happened at a particular stage. This matters because an audit needs checkable units, not a vague statement that data was used. The second idea is scoring contribution. A contribution score compresses a complicated training history into a number or ordered evidence about how much a sample mattered at checkpointed stages. Any such score involves a tradeoff: it gives an inspectable summary, but it cannot preserve every interaction among samples during training. The third idea is commitment from cryptography, where a record is bound to a compact fingerprint. If the record changes, the fingerprint no longer matches. The point is not to hide all information, but to make later tampering detectable while still allowing verification. There is also a systems tradeoff: the trace must spend time and storage to gain accountability. FG-Trac's claim of practical computational overhead says the accounting cost is meant to stay small enough that pipelines can keep training normally.
dots: This paper sits in the ML transparency family, but it attacks a different layer than many explanation papers. Some work tries to expose which concepts, graph paths, image regions, retrieved facts, or user-history pieces shaped a model decision. FG-Trac asks a more operational question: before explaining a decision, can the system prove what happened to the data that helped build the model? That connects it to the conference's recurring ideas about information, learning, privacy, security, and graph-based systems. The information idea appears because the pipeline must preserve the right facts about each sample while dropping enough detail to keep overhead practical. The learning idea appears because checkpoints mark how the model changes from examples over time. The security idea appears because cryptographic commitments make the history resistant to silent rewriting. Its multimodal graph experiment also links the work to graph learning, where data movement and sample influence can be harder to inspect than in a simple image pipeline.
ww: FG-Trac should work better than ordinary transparency because it records the relevant facts at the moment they occur. A post-hoc model explanation has to look backward from the final model and infer what might have mattered. A lifecycle trace instead follows the sample while the pipeline is running, so later questions can be answered from recorded events rather than reconstruction from memory. Checkpoints strengthen that record because they divide training into inspectable stages. If a sample is linked to the stages where the model state changed, contribution scores have a concrete anchor. Cryptographic commitments strengthen trust in a different way: they do not make the model smarter, but they make the evidence harder to rewrite without detection. The model-agnostic design is also important. If traceability required changing each architecture or loss objective, adoption would be limited and comparisons across pipelines would be messy. By sitting around the pipeline, FG-Trac can preserve ordinary training behavior while adding an audit trail.
po: The payoff is a machine learning pipeline that can furnish verifiable evidence about individual data samples. According to the abstract, FG-Trac can reconstruct complete and auditable data-usage histories, report whether a specific sample was used, identify when it was processed, and check whether records stayed intact over time. It does this while integrating without modifying model architectures or training objectives. The experiments on a canonical convolutional neural network and a multimodal graph learning pipeline show the intended breadth: the same traceability layer can support both a standard vision model and a more complex mixed-data graph setting, while preserving predictive performance and keeping overhead practical.
limits: The abstract does not prove that FG-Trac captures every kind of pipeline event an organization might care about, especially in larger distributed training systems, streaming data settings, or pipelines with many external tools. The contribution scores depend on the checkpoint design; if checkpoints are too sparse or poorly aligned with meaningful training changes, the scores may be less informative. Cryptographic commitments can show that a record changed, but they cannot guarantee that the original event was recorded honestly or completely. The method also assumes the added tracking overhead remains acceptable in real deployments. The experiments cover a convolutional neural network and a multimodal graph learning pipeline, but not every model family, governance setting, or adversarial audit scenario.
